newsitem.title: USA: Dole, Clinton make last-minute debate preparations.
newsitem.headline: Dole, Clinton make last-minute debate preparations.

text.p: Bob Dole turned on Saturday to former president George Bush for tips on Sunday's presidential debate while President Bill Clinton continued to talk down his chances of success and deflect a few lingering controversies ahead of the encounter.

Even though Bush was viewed as having lost his 1992 debates with Clinton, he "is the only Republican with experience debating Bill Clinton and we thought it was a good idea to get him down" to Bal Harbour, Florida, where Dole has been rehearsing, said Nelson Warfield, Dole's spokesman.

Clinton, meanwhile, has been preparing at a retreat in Chautauqua, in western New York, with former Maine Senator George Mitchell playing the role of Dole. Asked on Saturday whether he had got the better of Mitchell, Clinton replied, "Well, I don't know. Maybe I got him to a draw."
The televised 90-minute face-off, in Hartford, Connecticut, begins at 9 p.m. EDT on Sunday (0100 GMT on Monday). It is the first of two such confrontations between Dole and Clinton.

After conferring at Dole's seaside condominium, Bush and Dole, both dressed in blue blazers, collars open at the neck, emerged around the swimming pool to pronounce Dole ready for what Warfield called the "wily" Clinton.
"You reach a point where you just stop," Dole said of his preparation. "It's like filling up your tank with gas. It only holds so much."

Asked if had given Dole any particular pointers, Bush said: "Gosh no, he's ready. He doesn't need my tips." Asked how he thought he did in retrospect in the 1992 debates widely credited with having boosted Clinton, Bush said: "Well, I thought I did well, but maybe I didn't."

With Dole consistently lagging 10-20 points in opinion polls and only a month left before Election Day on Nov. 5, the Dole campaign portrayed the debate as one of the last, best opportunities to erase Clinton's lead.

"Tomorrow night is an important night for all Americans who are concerned about the future of our children, our families and our country," Dole said in his last pre-debate radio address. "Anyone who tunes in to the debate will quickly see that there are very real, distinct differences between my vision and plan for a better America and President Clinton's."

Anticipating a possible line of attack from Dole, Clinton on Saturday disclosed details of a controversial memo on the drug war from FBI Director Louis Freeh. He has refused to give the memo to congressional Republicans, citing executive privilege.

Pausing from his debate preparations, Clinton told reporters Freeh simply argues in the memo "that the federal government had never been properly orgainzed in terms of who had jurisdiction to do what in the drug war."
"He argues for a reallocation of authority and I thought argued quite persuasively that we needed a way to coordinate this," Clinton said.
Dole has made drugs a central theme of his campaign, often citing statistics that teenage drug use has doubled under Clinton and running television advertisments attacking the president on the issue.

In Bal Harbour, Warfield, Dole's spokesman, alluded to another possible line of attack, saying he expected the latest disclosures about the Clinton White House's controversial handling of FBI files to figure in the debate.

A former executive assistant in the White House security office, contradicting accounts by her old boss and co-workers, told Senate investigators this week that "everybody in the office knew" in the fall of 1993 that they were getting FBI files on "people who were no longer working there."
Asked about the report on Saturday, Clinton said: "I don't know anything about it other than what I saw in the paper today. I know nothing."
